Subject: Throughput floorplan & oscillation mitigation for Private GPU pool

Hi Laura,

Thanks again for taking this. IronGate is close to approving a private VPC deployment with Redwood, and before procurement we need to lock the capacity floorplan and a mitigation approach for the burst-induced oscillations we've been seeing in our staging cluster. I've attached a short capture of our expected traffic profile (load-profile-capture.csv) and a simple network schematic (network-topology.png). Summary of the workload: 

- Steady-state user traffic: 350-450 RPS sustained (chat-style conversational calls, average prompt length ~120 tokens).
- Regular daily spikes (marketing events + batch ingestion) that push to ~1,800-2,200 RPS for 2-8 minutes; many of those are 60s microbursts.
- Latency targets: p95 < 350 ms, p99 < 700 ms (app-level, includes network).
- Model families: one 13B instruction-tuned generator used for most sessions, and a fallback 33B-sized reranker used for heavy-lift requests. Both will be INT8 quantized for inference.

Key asks from our side:
1) A recommended GPU pool footprint (node counts by GPU type) for hitting the steady-state and absorbing 2x-5x short bursts without violating p99.
2) Admission & smoothing controls (server-side) you recommend to avoid capacity oscillation when we hit burst windows.
3) Network/topology checklist so we don't hit egress/NIC bottlenecks during surges.

We want to avoid buying 2-3x capacity just to cover spikes; if we can control the tails with smart smoothing, that's ideal. Can you propose a floorplan and an ops runbook we can include with the purchase approval?

Thanks,
Samir

Hi Samir —

Appreciate the profile and schematic. We sketched an initial floorplan (attached: initial-floorplan-draft.pdf) and a set of mitigation layers that avoid a pure overprovision approach. High-level recommendations up front:

- Baseline: 8 H100-80GB nodes (64 GPUs) configured as two availability subclusters (4 nodes / subcluster) to give fault isolation and headroom for upgrades. This yields ~420-550 sustained RPS for the 13B generator with conservative batching and quantization.
- Burst absorb / smoothing: reserve a 2-node (16 GPU) warm standby pool for fast handoff, plus a short-lived preemptible burst group (up to 4 nodes) we can spin up from the private cloud overlay within 45-90s depending on provisioning path. Together this gives the ability to absorb up to ~1.9k RPS before backend queuing is required.
- Admission control & smoothing: combine token-budgeting (per-API-key soft limits), request shaping at the edge (leaky-bucket per-route), and quick prefix caching for repeated conversational tokens to reduce repeated decode compute during spikes. Important: add a short (30-120s) client-side retry-backoff + server-side 429 with Retry-After to avoid thundering herds.
- Graceful degradation: during sustained >2k RPS pressures, fall back noisily to the 13B distilled variant and rate-limit heavy reranker calls asynchronously (return provisional responses and enqueue high-cost work).

Network checklist (top items):
- Use 25G+ NICs per GPU host; plan egress per-node at ~6-8 Gbps under worst-case token emission (assuming large decode outputs).
- Set MTU to 9000 if supported; enable flow control and tune receive buffers on the host network stack.
- Ensure route table avoids hairpinning through shared transit gateways during bursts; prefer direct paths to egress.
- DSCP tagging for inference traffic (so top-of-rack switches can prioritize control plane and p95-sensitive flows).

I've looped David and Jonas for the micro-sizing math and an ops runbook draft. Can you confirm your procurement timeline (target order by end of June?) and whether you can accept the 45-90s burst spin-up window or need sub-10s cold-start guarantees?

Next steps proposed:
- Jonas/David: produce a per-GPU throughput map + warm-pool sizing doc.
- We (Redwood): deliver admission control policy examples and a staging test plan to validate oscillation behavior.

Thanks — attaching the initial-floorplan-draft.pdf with the rough node/zone split and expected qps curves.

Best,
Laura Bennett
Head of Product, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Throughput floorplan & oscillation mitigation for Private GPU pool (math)

Folks — quick sizing notes and assumptions so IronGate has concrete numbers for procurement:

Assumptions:
- 13B INT8 generator: avg token-latency per-token on H100-80GB ~0.7 ms (batched 8-12), effective throughput per GPU ~60 RPS (full request/response, ~120 tokens output average).
- 33B INT8 reranker: avg per-request latency ~25-40 ms (larger memory, smaller batching), effective throughput per GPU ~12-16 RPS.
- Network overhead: assume 10% end-to-end time budget.

Baseline steady-state math:
- Need to sustain 450 RPS generator QPS => 450 / 60 ≈ 7.5 GPUs => 8 GPUs (~1 node if 8 GPUs/node). We propose 64 GPUs (8 nodes): gives ~3.5x baseline buffer for the generator under conservative batching and degradation.

Burst handling:
- 2-node warm pool (16 GPUs) held hot: absorbs additional ~960 RPS. Combined with baseline 64 GPUs that gives ~1,600 RPS of generated capacity before significant queuing — close to the lower bound of their reported bursts.
- Add preemptible 4-node burst group (32 GPUs) as elastic capacity for short events; spin up time depends on infra (image pull, device binding) — 45-90s realistic. That brings theoretical headroom to ~2,700 RPS if fully provisioned.

Smoothing strategy (ops knobs):
- Admission control: implement per-route leaky-bucket set to steady-state + 20% headroom, with a separate short-burst token bucket allowing up to burst_limit over 60s.
- Buffering / queue depth: cap in-flight request depth per GPU to prevent OOM; maintain a small request queue with probabilistic early-drop when average queue wait > 80 ms.
- Caching & warm pools: prefix KV caching reduces compute for repeated conversational context by ~10-25% in our tests.

Risk items and mitigations:
- Cold spin-up: if provisioning path uses images from remote registry, pre-pull images and keep warm standby to hit the 45s SL.
- Network egress saturation: if customers emit long responses at scale, cap tokens per response or stream with backpressure.
- Reranker load: offload reranker calls to asynchronous pipelines where possible; allocate a dedicated 8-GPU partition for reranker during peak windows.

I will put these numbers in a short spreadsheet and attach to the runbook. If IronGate is constrained on budget, we can reduce warm standby and increase burst spin-up + client-side backoff, but that will raise p99 risk during the first 60s of a spike.

-David

Sr. Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Samir / IronGate team —

Thanks for the profile and for the prompt responses from Laura/David. Quick operational plan and timeline we recommend so your procurement pack can include an ops-ready mitigation plan: 

1) Today: Redwood delivers the per-GPU throughput spreadsheet (David) + an ops runbook with admission-control policy examples and a staging test plan (Jonas).
2) By 2026-06-04: IronGate agrees to one of two procurement options:
   a) Conservative: 8 baseline nodes + 2 warm-standby + 4 preemptible nodes (recommended for minimal p99 risk).
   b) Budget-tight: 6 baseline nodes + 1 warm-standby + 2 preemptible nodes + stricter client-side throttles.
3) By 2026-06-18: Staging validation: run 60/120/600s burst tests (1.8k -> 2.2k RPS) to validate p95/p99 and network egress behavior. We'll run with and without reranker offload to quantify degradation.
4) Pre-procurement deliverable: a one-page wiring/network checklist (25G NICs, jumbo frames, DSCP tagging, reserved egress lanes) and a configuration snippet for admission control in the Redwood agent.

Please reply with which procurement option you prefer and whether the ~45-90s warm spin-up window is acceptable; if you require sub-30s guarantees we need to discuss additional cold-warm strategies (hot-standby per-zone) and cost implications.

I'll attach the runbook links to the HubSpot record (IG-0347) and drop the spreadsheet in the Drive folder.

-Jonas
